title: Number Sense & Estimation
coreInsight: Numbers carry magnitude and structure; estimation and reasonableness can reveal what an exact answer should look like before calculation.
targetLearnerRealization: Before calculating exactly, magnitude and structure can eliminate impossible answers and suggest an efficient path.
learningObjectives: Estimate products by replacing awkward factors with nearby friendly numbers.
Use bounds and place value to reject impossible results.
Decide when an estimate settles a question and when exact calculation is still needed.
Transfer estimation to a rate and unit-conversion setting.

closingSeeds: Magnitude can be located before a number is written exactly.
Whole-number marks leave unnamed positions between them on a number line.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Exact calculation is always better than estimation.
An answer that comes from valid arithmetic does not need a reasonableness check.
The written form of a number is more important than its magnitude or structure.

beats.purpose: Create a need to judge scale before doing exact multiplication.
beats.expectedRealization: The leading digits and place values locate a product's scale without an exact calculation.
beats.transitionIn: Three products are deliberately awkward. Place each one in the right neighborhood before multiplying exactly.
beats.transitionOut: A product's neighborhood can be known before its exact address.
beats.prompt: Sort each product into the neighborhood where its value belongs. Estimate—do not calculate each exact product.

response.feedback: Replace each factor with a nearby number that is easy to multiply.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Friendly factors reveal all three scales without exact multiplication.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Try 50 × 20, 400 × 20, and 2,000 × 50. Compare the number of zeros in those products.

visual.ariaLabel: The three products grouped into neighborhoods near one thousand, ten thousand, and one hundred thousand

steps.title: Keep the size
steps.body: Round each factor to a nearby friendly number, then multiply the friendly pair.

steps.title: Read place value
steps.body: The three estimates land in different place-value neighborhoods, so exact arithmetic is unnecessary for this sort.

resolution.takeaway: Estimate first when the scale alone can settle the question.

beats.purpose: Surface an absurd calculator-style result and make bounds override blind trust in written arithmetic.
beats.expectedRealization: A result outside simple bounds is impossible even if it looks calculator-produced.
beats.transitionIn: Use the first product's neighborhood to inspect a result instead of recomputing it.
beats.prompt: A display reports 48 × 19 = 9,120. Which check proves immediately that the display is wrong?
beats.correctFeedback: Right. The simple upper bound makes 9,120 impossible.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Look for a statement that puts the actual product below a known number.

steps.title: Build an upper bound
steps.body: Both factors are positive, with 48 < 50 and 19 < 20. Therefore 48 × 19 < 50 × 20 = 1,000.

steps.title: Reject the display
steps.body: Since 9,120 is greater than 1,000, it cannot be the product. The exact value is 912, but the bound already settled the question.

beats.purpose: Practice choosing nearby factors that preserve magnitude and simplify multiplication.
beats.expectedRealization: Useful rounding changes the numbers a little while making the structure much easier.
beats.transitionIn: A bound can reject a result. A well-chosen estimate can also predict one.
beats.prompt: Which friendly-number product gives the most useful quick estimate for 612 × 39?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Both replacements stay close and make the product immediate.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Preserve the place value of each factor and change each number as little as practical.

steps.title: Round nearby
steps.body: 612 is close to 600, and 39 is close to 40.

steps.title: Use the easy structure
steps.body: 6 × 4 = 24, then the three zeros give 24,000. The exact product, 23,868, is close to the estimate.

resolution.takeaway: Friendly numbers should simplify the work without changing the scale.

beats.purpose: Name estimation and reasonableness only after learners have used both ideas.
beats.expectedRealization: An estimate is a deliberate nearby value that predicts or checks an exact result.
beats.transitionIn: The same move sorted products, rejected an impossible display, and predicted a result.
beats.name: Estimation and reasonableness
beats.conciseDefinition: An estimate replaces quantities with nearby, easier ones to predict magnitude. A reasonableness check compares a result with that prediction or with reliable bounds.
beats.formalization: nearby friendly factors → easy product → expected scale
beats.memoryHook: Control the size before chasing the digits.

beats.purpose: Apply factor rounding in an authentic contest problem designed to be solved by approximation.
beats.expectedRealization: Opposite-looking decimal and whole-number scales can recombine into a manageable product.
beats.transitionIn: Now the two factors look much less friendly, but their leading digits and place values still control the product.
beats.whyNow: The learner has chosen friendly factors and used scale checks; this contest problem makes approximation the intended solution rather than a fallback.
beats.entryBridge: Round each factor to one useful leading digit, then compare the estimate with the answer choices.
beats.exitBridge: The estimate selected a widely separated choice without requiring the exact product.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Nearby friendly-number cards carried from the opening estimates.
learnerPrompts: Before advancing the animation, what nearby numbers preserve the size of both factors?
After the factors shift, combine their leading digits and powers of ten. Which answer choice has that magnitude?
beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. 0.0003 × 8,000,000 = 2,400, so choice D is closest.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Track both the leading digits and place value: 3 × 8 = 24, while 0.0001 × 1,000,000 = 100.

steps.title: Multiply the friendly numbers
steps.body: Three ten-thousandths times eight million is 2,400.

steps.title: Use the choice spacing
steps.body: The choices are far apart in magnitude. An estimate near 2,400 identifies D; exact multiplication would add work without changing the decision.

resolution.takeaway: When choices are widely separated, magnitude can be enough.

beats.purpose: Distinguish a question settled by estimation from one whose close options require exact calculation.
beats.expectedRealization: Estimation controls the answer but does not always finish the answer.
beats.transitionIn: The contest choices were far apart. Move them close together and ask what the same estimate can still prove.
beats.prompt: For 247 × 31, the estimate 250 × 30 = 7,500 is quick. The choices are 7,500, 7,600, 7,657, and 7,750. What should you do next?

options.text: Choose 7,500 because an estimate is always the answer.
Calculate more exactly because several choices are near 7,500.
Choose 7,750 because estimates always round down.
Reject every choice because none equals 250 × 30.

beats.correctFeedback: Right. The estimate narrows the search, but the close choices demand exact work.
beats.incorrectFeedback: An estimate predicts a neighborhood. Check whether only one choice occupies that neighborhood.

steps.title: Use the estimate
steps.body: A result around 7,500 is plausible, but all four choices are close enough that magnitude alone does not decide.

resolution.takeaway: Estimate first; calculate exactly when the remaining choices are too close.

beats.purpose: Transfer magnitude control to a rate, time, and unit-conversion setting.
beats.expectedRealization: Estimation remains useful when a product must be interpreted and converted before rounding.
beats.transitionIn: The next estimate is not just a bare product: its units must travel from feet per second to feet and then to miles.
beats.whyNow: After pure product estimation and a decision about exactness, the same habit must survive rate language, units, and rounding to the nearest half-mile.
beats.entryBridge: First estimate how many feet sound covers in ten seconds; then compare that distance with miles.
beats.exitBridge: The units changed, but the same magnitude check kept the final rounding under control.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A scale of nearby values, now labeled in feet and miles.
learnerPrompts: Before advancing, about how many feet does sound travel in 10 seconds?
After the distance appears in feet, use about 5,000 feet per mile to predict the number of miles.
When 2.06 appears, compare its distance from 2 and 2.5 before choosing.
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The sound travels about two miles, and 2.06 is nearer 2 than 2.5.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Multiply the rate by 10 seconds, then remember that one mile is a little more than 5,000 feet. Round to the nearest half-mile, not automatically upward.

steps.title: Find the distance
steps.body: The sound travels for 10 seconds at 1,088 feet per second.

steps.title: Predict the miles
steps.body: Since 10,880 is a little more than twice 5,280, the distance should be a little more than 2 miles.

steps.title: Convert and round
steps.body: 10,880 ÷ 5,280 ≈ 2.06 miles. This is closer to 2 than to 2.5, so the answer is C.

resolution.takeaway: Carry units through the estimate, then round to the nearest allowed value.

beats.purpose: Consolidate estimation as a decision-making tool rather than a substitute for all exact arithmetic.
beats.expectedRealization: A complete estimation habit predicts scale, checks plausibility, and notices when precision is still needed.
beats.transitionIn: Across a display check, a contest product, and a distance, the estimate did different jobs.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a strong estimate-first habit? Select every one that applies.

options.text: Predict the answer's scale with nearby friendly numbers.
Reject a result that violates reliable bounds.
Calculate more exactly if several choices remain plausible.
Trust any exact-looking display without checking it.
Always replace the exact answer with the estimate.

response.feedback: An estimate may predict, check, or narrow a result; it does not automatically replace exact work.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Estimate first to control the answer, then use only as much precision as the question needs.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep actions that use magnitude to guide or check work. Remove claims that an estimate is always final or that a display needs no check.

steps.title: Predict
steps.body: Nearby friendly numbers reveal the likely scale.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Bounds can expose impossible results even before an exact recalculation.

steps.title: Decide
steps.body: Widely separated choices may need only an estimate; close choices may require exact work.

resolution.takeaway: Control the size before chasing the digits.

beats.purpose: Create a forward question about naming magnitudes that lie between whole numbers.
beats.expectedRealization: Whole-number labels do not name every possible position on a number line.
beats.transitionIn: Magnitude tells us where a number lives. But whole-number marks do not name every possible location.
beats.prompt: A measured length lands strictly between 2 and 3 on this line. What new need does that create?

visual.ariaLabel: A number line with whole-number marks zero through four and unmarked positions between them

options.text: We need ways to name and compare quantities between whole numbers.
The length must actually equal 2 or 3.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The gap contains real magnitudes that need names and comparisons.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The measurement exists even though no whole-number tick names its exact position.

steps.body: A point between 2 and 3 has a definite magnitude, but neither neighboring whole number names it exactly. Fractions and decimals will let us name those positions; percents will give another way to describe the same quantities.

resolution.takeaway: The number line continues inside every whole-number gap.

notes: The generated opening isolates magnitude before formal vocabulary or contextual load.
The approved 2017 problem is guided because approximation is the intended method; the approved 2001 problem supplies independent transfer through rate, units, and rounding.
